posts.title: Microsoft releases new Nvidia-chip AI PCs with revamped Windows 11 | TechCrunch
posts.author: Julie Bort
posts.summary: Microsoft unveiled two new AI‑ready PCs powered by Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip at its San Francisco Tech Week event. The Surface Laptop Ultra starts at $2,600 and can reach $5,900, while the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box begins at $6,000 and ships with developer tools such as VS Code and GitHub Copilot. Both devices run a revamped Windows 11 that includes “Execution Containers” to sandbox AI agents, a feature Microsoft says will be available to all users. The announcement also highlighted a $1,000 trade‑in incentive for MacBook Pro owners and noted Dell’s concurrent release of the XPS 16 Creator Edition.
key_points: Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra and RTX Spark Dev Box use Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip to run AI models locally
The devices ship with a new Windows 11 version featuring Execution Containers for sandboxing AI agents
Microsoft offers a $1,000 trade‑in for MacBook Pro owners to encourage developers to switch
Dell also announced its XPS 16 Creator Edition with similar specs

posts.title: OpenAI’s Alexander Embiricos is coming to Disrupt 2026 | TechCrunch
posts.author: TechCrunch Events
posts.summary: OpenAI’s product lead Alexander Embiricos will speak at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, where he will discuss the company’s new personal AI agents called Dots, unveiled after the chatbot launch. Dots are designed to run continuously, connect to everyday apps, and pursue goals in the background, giving AI deeper access to users’ work and digital lives. Embiricos will address the autonomy, privacy, and trust challenges that arise when AI can act on behalf of users. The session, titled “What Comes After the Chatbot?”, will take place on the AI Stage at Moscone West in San Francisco from October 13‑15.
key_points: OpenAI is positioning Dots as the next evolution beyond chatbots, offering continuous, background AI agents that integrate with users’ apps.
The company is grappling with questions of autonomy, privacy, and trust as these agents gain deeper access to personal data.
Alexander Embiricos will discuss these issues and the future of personal AI at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026.

posts.title: How to find out if Amazon thinks you have 'flat buttocks' | TechCrunch
posts.author: Amanda Silberling
posts.summary: Amazon’s user profile page reveals inferred traits about shoppers, including a surprising claim that a user has "flat buttocks" based on purchases such as butt scrunch leggings. The article explains how to access and edit these preferences on both desktop and mobile, and notes that other users have found Amazon’s assumptions accurate or amusing. A viral Threads post about the profile sparked widespread curiosity and highlighted how much personal data e‑commerce giants collect. The piece underscores growing concerns about data privacy and the intimate surveillance that tech companies can perform on consumers.
key_points: Amazon displays inferred traits like "flat buttocks" in user profiles
Users can view and edit preferences via account settings on desktop and mobile
A viral Threads post sparked discussion on data privacy and Amazon’s profiling
Tech companies’ detailed profiling raises surveillance concerns

posts.title: Healthleap raises $38M for its AI that flags hospital patients who may need a closer look | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ram Iyer
posts.summary: Healthleap, a South African startup founded by siblings Jemima and Josiah Meyer, has secured $38 million in seed and Series A funding to advance its AI platform that scans hospital electronic health records for patients at risk of undiagnosed conditions such as malnutrition and delirium. The platform, which pulls structured data and unstructured clinician notes through language models, is already deployed in more than 50 hospitals including Penn Medicine and Cedars‑Sinai, and has helped hospitals achieve a 5‑to‑20‑fold return on investment. The company’s revenue has grown over tenfold in the past year, and its contracts are priced by licensed bed count with an outcome‑based model that guarantees measurable ROI. Healthleap plans to use the new capital to engineer additional condition‑identification modules, expand to outpatient and home‑care settings, and ultimately cover more than 40 major health conditions.
key_points: $38 million raised: $8 million seed led by Sequoia Capital and First Round Capital, $30 million Series A led by Hummingbird Ventures
AI platform extracts clinical notes and structured data to flag patients with malnutrition, delirium, aspiration pneumonia, pressure ulcers and readmission risk, deployed in 50+ hospitals
Customers report 5‑to‑20‑fold ROI; at the University of Pennsylvania the malnutrition program generated $23.8 million in annualized financial impact
Healthleap will invest in engineering, sales and customer success to add more conditions and expand into outpatient and home‑care markets

posts.title: 6 days to Disrupt 2026: Save on your pass before doors open | TechCrunch
posts.author: TechCrunch Events
posts.summary: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 will open on Oct. 13 in San Francisco’s Moscone West, and the final day to register for discounted passes is Oct. 2. Attendees can save up to $100 on tickets, bring a colleague for 50% off a second pass, or grab a $75 Expo+ Pass if they’ve been laid off. The three‑day expo will feature more than 200 sessions across six stages, 250 tech leaders, and a Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition offering a $100,000 prize. Highlights include speakers from OpenAI, Rivian, NVIDIA, and Anthropic, and a focus on AI, fintech, robotics, infrastructure, product, hiring, and scaling.
key_points: Last day to register is Oct. 2 with discounts up to $100
Bring a colleague for 50% off a second pass
$75 Expo+ Pass available for laid‑off attendees
Over 200 sessions, 250 leaders, and a $100,000 Startup Battlefield 200 prize

posts.title: SpaceX alumni nab $100M to rethink shipping with autonomous freight trains | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant
posts.summary: Parallel Systems, a startup founded by former SpaceX engineers, has raised $100 million in a Series C round to scale its autonomous freight train, the Panther, which can haul several tons of cargo up to 500 miles without an operator. The vehicle’s battery‑powered, coupler‑free design lets it travel in short, uncoupled platoons, reducing congestion and emissions while enabling railroads to regain competitiveness on short‑haul routes that now largely belong to trucking. Parallel has already earned Federal Railroad Administration approval to run near the Port of Savannah, where it has tested safety controls on 160 miles of track, and it aims to bring its first commercial payload to market soon. By offering predictable, congestion‑free deliveries, the company hopes to attract trucking firms and help railroads recapture a sizable share of the $1 trillion surface freight market.
key_points: Parallel Systems raised $100 million to scale its autonomous Panther freight train, targeting short‑haul routes under 500 miles.
The Panther’s battery‑powered, coupler‑free platoon design reduces congestion and emissions, offering railroads a competitive alternative to trucking.
The startup has already received Federal Railroad Administration approval and is testing its system near the Port of Savannah, aiming for commercial rollout soon.

posts.title: Tony Fadell on why the first wave of AI gadgets failed — and what comes next | TechCrunch
posts.author: Amanda Silberling
posts.summary: Tony Fadell, the "father of the iPod" and former Nest founder, warned at MIT Future Fest that the first wave of AI gadgets failed because they offered cool tech without solving real consumer problems. He argued that trust and privacy are the biggest hurdles for personal AI assistants, insisting that on‑device processing is essential to protect sensitive data. Fadell highlighted Apple’s hardware advantage and its reputation for privacy as a potential path forward, while noting that companies like Meta and OpenAI must build dedicated devices to access the sensors they need. He cautioned that startups have only one shot at product‑market fit, making the stakes higher than for established firms.
key_points: Early AI devices failed because they did not address real consumer pain points.
Trust and privacy, especially on‑device data handling, are critical for personal AI assistants.
Apple’s hardware and privacy reputation give it an edge, but it lacks proprietary AI models.
Startups face a single‑shot risk; a misstep can end the company.

posts.title: Google experiments with an AI-powered gaming platform | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lauren Forristal
posts.summary: Google Labs has unveiled Playground, an AI‑powered platform that lets users build browser‑based games from simple text prompts without coding. Creators choose genre, 2D or 3D, single‑ or multiplayer, and can upload visuals that the AI turns into game assets, then publish or share games on a free Explore gallery. The service uses a weekly token system, with a free tier and higher limits for Google One AI subscribers, and Google plans to add Unity Spark integration for advanced 3D and professional mechanics. Playground joins a growing field of AI‑assisted game‑development tools, following moves by Roblox and building on Google’s earlier gaming initiatives such as Stadia and YouTube Playables.
key_points: Google Labs launched Playground, an AI‑driven game‑creation tool that requires no coding.
Users can design 2D/3D, single/multi‑player games via text prompts and upload visuals for AI‑generated assets.
The platform uses a token‑based model, offers free and Google One AI tiers, and will soon integrate Unity Spark for enhanced 3D capabilities.

posts.title: Spotify expands audiobooks to over 180 markets | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta
posts.summary: Spotify has rolled out its audiobook service to more than 180 markets worldwide, bringing the catalog to over 350,000 titles in 120 languages and making it available to an estimated 750 million users. The expansion, which began today, adds a Premium‑tier 12‑hour listening allowance in several countries and a stand‑alone Audiobook+ subscription that already has over 1 million subscribers and $100 million in annual recurring revenue. Spotify also continues to grow its audiobook ecosystem with features like Page Match, an AI‑powered author tool, and experiments with physical book sales in select markets. The move positions the music‑streaming giant to compete more directly with dedicated audiobook platforms such as Audible.
key_points: Spotify expands audiobooks to 180+ markets with 350,000 titles in 120 languages
Premium 12‑hour allowance and Audiobook+ subscription bring 1 million users and $100 million ARR
Page Match, AI author tool, and physical book sales experiments broaden the platform
Monthly audiobook listeners grew 40% and listening hours 30% in the past year

posts.title: The full Disrupt 2026 breakout session agenda revealed | TechCrunch
posts.author: TechCrunch Events

The agenda covers emerging AI themes such as physical AI, inference economics, and AI in space, featuring speakers from SOSV, Anthropic, and The Aerospace Corporation

Discounted passes and Expo+ options are available to encourage broader participation

posts.title: Apple is reportedly partnering with LG to launch a smart lock, thermostat, and doorbell | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lucas Ropek
posts.summary: Apple is partnering with LG to launch a new line of smart home devices, including a smart lock, thermostat, and doorbell, that will integrate with its upcoming smart home hub slated for release on October 13. The hub will feature a 6‑inch square display that can be mounted on a wall or placed on a countertop. LG‑branded devices are expected to be announced next week, and Apple and LG are also developing indoor and outdoor security cameras and a floodlight. The collaboration positions Apple to compete more directly with Amazon’s Ring and other smart‑home ecosystems.
key_points: Apple and LG are collaborating on a smart lock, thermostat, and doorbell that will integrate with Apple’s new smart home hub
The devices will carry the LG brand even though they are jointly developed
Apple’s smart home hub, featuring a 6‑inch display, is expected to launch on October 13
Security cameras and a floodlight are also in development as part of the partnership

posts.title: Ex-Ramp engineers raise $20M for platform Melius after scrapping their first product | TechCrunch
posts.author: Marina Temkin
posts.summary: Melius, an AI platform that creates ad campaigns, images, and videos, announced it has raised a total of $25 million, including a $20 million Series A led by CRV and a $5 million seed round led by General Catalyst. The company was founded by former Ramp engineers Joowon Kim, Young Kim, and Arnav Ramu, who abandoned their original ad‑spend tool after six months and rebuilt the product from scratch as an "agents lab for creative work." Within two months of emerging from stealth in July, Melius reported more than $1 million in annualized revenue and is positioning itself in a large market that also includes competitors such as Higgsfield, Krea, and Flora AI. The founders view the crowded space as a sign of strong demand and believe multiple players can thrive.
key_points: Melius secured $25 million in funding, led by CRV and General Catalyst.
The founders pivoted from an ad‑spend tool to an AI creative‑generation platform after scrapping the original code.
The startup achieved over $1 million ARR in just two months after launch.
Competition includes Higgsfield, Krea, and Flora AI, but the founders see room for many players in the market.

posts.title: The next hurdle for AI agents: getting websites to let them in | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Personal AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, Instinct, and ChatGPT’s Dots are gaining traction for booking flights, ordering groceries, and making purchases, but many retailers are blocking them from completing transactions. Amazon recently prevented Muse from browsing or buying on its site, and Walmart’s anti‑bot verification steps have also caused agents to fail, even though Walmart claims the blocks are unintentional. In response, Meta, Walmart, Stripe, Sierra, Genesys, Rocket, NiCE, and Decagon are collaborating on an open standard to distinguish legitimate user‑driven bots from malicious ones and enable secure agent‑to‑agent commerce. Meanwhile, other companies such as Delta, United, eBay, Yelp, and Cloudflare have either restricted or are evaluating how to allow AI agents, highlighting the growing friction between consumer convenience and web‑security practices.
key_points: Amazon has blocked Meta’s Muse from its retail site, preventing AI‑driven purchases
Walmart’s human‑verification bot can inadvertently block AI agents, though the company says the block is unintentional
Meta and partners are developing an open standard to allow safe, authenticated AI agent interactions with businesses
Cloudflare’s crawler policy change in September 2023 may be contributing to increased AI agent blocking on many sites

posts.title: Hark releases an AI personal assistant with a focus on privacy | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim Fernholz
posts.summary: Hark, a startup founded by Brett Adcock, has launched Hark Pro, an AI personal assistant that operates as a full‑screen interface designed to act as an operating system for the computer. The assistant is trained specifically for computer use, allowing it to manage email, calendar, files, and even complete web tasks while displaying its navigation to build trust and emphasize privacy. Hark positions itself against larger players like Meta and OpenAI by promising no ads or data mining, and it plans to release an AI‑native device in 2027. The product’s focus on privacy, task‑specific intelligence, and a transparent user experience distinguishes it in the crowded AI assistant market.
key_points: Hark Pro is a full‑screen AI assistant trained for computer use, handling email, calendar, files, and web tasks.
The interface shows the assistant’s web navigation to build trust and avoid data mining, positioning Hark against Meta and OpenAI.
Hark plans to launch an AI‑native device in 2027 to complement its software.
The startup emphasizes privacy and task‑specific help rather than broad LLM capabilities.

posts.title: India's JioHotstar takes partnership route for Middle East expansion | TechCrunch
posts.author: Jagmeet Singh
posts.summary: JioHotstar, the Reliance‑backed streaming service with over 500 million monthly users, is expanding into the Middle East and North Africa through a partnership with Starzplay, giving the platform a dedicated section for Indian films, shows, originals and reality franchises in multiple languages. The move follows JioHotstar’s earlier launches in the U.K., Canada and Singapore, but unlike those markets the MENA rollout will not include its own sports content; instead a bundled sports plan with Starzplay’s cricket offering is priced at AED 49.99 (about $13.60) per month. The partnership taps the region’s large South‑Asian diaspora, allowing new JioHotstar originals to premiere simultaneously with India and offering audio in up to ten languages, with a particular focus on Malayalam programming.
key_points: JioHotstar partners with Starzplay to launch a dedicated Indian content section in MENA
The MENA rollout excludes JioHotstar’s sports library but offers a bundled sports plan at AED 49.99/month
New originals will premiere simultaneously with India and feature audio in up to ten languages
The strategy targets the region’s large South‑Asian diaspora, especially the Malayali community

posts.title: Facebook tests going Reels-first in India | TechCrunch
posts.author: Jagmeet Singh
posts.summary: Meta is testing a Reels‑first user experience in India that launches users directly into full‑screen video when they open the app, with a similar test underway in Indonesia. Users who are part of the test can opt out and switch back to the traditional feed, which remains available as a second tab. The move follows Meta’s broader strategy to make video the centerpiece of Facebook, a shift that has already seen all new videos posted as Reels and the app’s Video tab renamed to Reels. India, Meta’s largest market with over 400 million users, is a key testing ground for this video‑centric approach.
key_points: Meta is testing a Reels‑first UX in India and Indonesia that opens users directly into full‑screen video
Users can opt out and return to the classic feed, which remains a second tab
The test is part of Meta’s strategy to make video central to Facebook, with all new videos posted as Reels

posts.title: How AI decision models could change content moderation | TechCrunch
posts.author: Russell Brandom
posts.summary: Musubi has unveiled PolicyLM-1.7B, a lightweight decision model designed for real‑time content moderation that can apply plain‑English policies to messages in under 50 milliseconds. The model, released with open weights, offers the speed and cost of traditional AI classifiers while retaining the flexibility of a large language model, and it does not require retraining when policies change. This launch follows the recent surge in decision‑model research, highlighted by TypeSafe AI’s Jev and similar offerings from OpenAI and Amazon, which aim to deliver faster, cheaper outcomes by limiting outputs to predetermined choices. By enabling platform managers to label content proactively and iteratively, PolicyLM-1.7B could significantly streamline moderation workflows and adapt quickly to evolving policy needs.
key_points: PolicyLM-1.7B is a real‑time, open‑weight decision model that applies plain‑English content policies in under 50 ms.
It matches the cost and speed of existing classifiers but adds LLM flexibility, eliminating the need for retraining when policies change.
The release follows a broader industry shift toward decision models like Jev, OpenAI’s and Amazon’s offerings, which prioritize speed and cost over full text generation.
Musubi’s approach could transform content moderation by providing scalable, customizable labeling that adapts quickly to policy updates.

posts.title: AI computing startup Lambda to raise $4B ahead of planned IPO | TechCrunch
posts.author: Rebecca Bellan
posts.summary: Lambda, a cloud provider focused on GPU capacity for AI workloads, is raising up to $4 billion at a $14.5 billion pre‑money valuation, likely its last private round before a planned 2027 IPO. The round is led by Coatue Management and Blackstone, and the company’s backlog surged from $15 billion in June to $50 billion in September, largely because of a $35 billion commitment from Anthropic. While the deal fuels Lambda’s valuation, it also highlights the company’s reliance on a single large client amid a market where lenders are tightening credit for data‑center buildouts. The fresh capital will position Lambda for a future public listing and give it a stronger footing as it competes with other Nvidia‑backed neoclouds such as CoreWeave and Nebius.
key_points: Lambda is raising up to $4 billion at a $14.5 billion pre‑money valuation ahead of a 2027 IPO
Its backlog jumped from $15 billion to $50 billion, driven largely by a $35 billion deal with Anthropic
The funding round, led by Coatue and Blackstone, provides capital to navigate debt‑lender scrutiny for data‑center expansion
Lambda joins other Nvidia‑backed neoclouds that rely on large AI contracts to fund growth

posts.title: Paramount closes historic Warner Bros. merger to form Skydance | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aisha Malik
posts.summary: Paramount has finalized its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, creating a new company called Skydance that will combine Paramount+ and HBO Max with networks such as CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central and Food Network. The merger brings major franchises—including The Lord of the Rings, Game of Thrones, the DC Universe and Yellowstone—under Skydance’s control and will generate annual revenue of nearly $70 billion. David Ellison, who recently merged Skydance Media with Paramount, will lead the new entity, which will trade on the NYSE under the ticker SKYD. The deal was cleared after settlements with U.S. states and the Writers Guild, marking one of the largest entertainment mergers ever.
key_points: Paramount’s $110 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery creates Skydance, merging Paramount+ and HBO Max with major cable networks and franchises
The new company will generate about $70 billion in annual revenue and trade on the NYSE as SKYD
David Ellison, backed by the Ellison family’s Oracle wealth, will head Skydance after previously merging Skydance Media with Paramount

posts.title: Hot Girl Hotline is like 'Dear Abby' for the AI era | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Hot Girl Hotline, founded by sisters Baila Mudgil and Sumrin, offers a privacy‑focused AI chat that gives young women behavioral‑science‑based dating and relationship advice. The service prioritizes safety by flagging harmful conversations, providing crisis‑hotline referrals, and using zero‑data‑retention policies. It charges $9.99 a month and plans to expand beyond relationship advice into beauty and lifestyle. The startup will showcase its product at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 and is already bootstrapped with paying users.
key_points: Hot Girl Hotline delivers AI‑powered dating advice grounded in behavioral science while emphasizing user safety and privacy
The founders, sisters Baila Mudgil and Sumrin, use zero‑data‑retention and crisis‑hotline referrals to mitigate mental‑health risks
The service monetizes with a $9.99/month subscription and aims to broaden into beauty and lifestyle categories
It will debut at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 and already has a paying user base

posts.title: Silicon Valley's AI wunderkind launches Underdog, the most private Instinct/Muse competitor yet | TechCrunch
posts.author: Julie Bort
posts.summary: Sigil Wen, a self‑taught coder who grew up hacking alongside future AI leaders, has launched Underdog, an invite‑only beta of a private on‑device AI assistant that keeps all user data on Macs, Windows PCs, and soon Linux, iPhone, and Android. Powered by Wen’s Husky inference engine and a 27‑billion‑parameter model fine‑tuned from Qwen3.8‑27B, Underdog offers privacy‑centric features such as encrypted account keys while matching the performance of larger cloud‑hosted models like Claude Opus 4.6. The startup plans to remain free and ad‑free, instead taking a tiny fee on Stripe‑powered payment transactions, a model that aligns the AI’s revenue with user spending rather than data collection. Backed by investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Khosla Ventures, and Stripe co‑founder Patrick Collison, Underdog aims to prove that privacy and capability can coexist in consumer AI.
key_points: Underdog is a private on‑device AI assistant that runs a 27‑billion‑parameter model entirely on user hardware via the Husky engine.
It preserves privacy by keeping data on the device and encrypting account keys, while matching the performance of larger cloud models.
The business model is free and ad‑free, taking only a small fee on Stripe transactions instead of charging subscriptions or selling data.
The startup is backed by prominent investors such as Andreessen Horowitz, Khosla Ventures, and Stripe co‑founder Patrick Collison.

posts.title: Furientis lands $25M from Benchmark to mass-produce low-cost missile interceptors | TechCrunch
posts.author: Marina Temkin
posts.summary: Benchmark has led a $25 million seed round for Furientis, a one‑year‑old defense startup that aims to mass‑produce low‑cost interceptor missiles. The company, valued at $125 million, already secured a Pentagon contract and has launched dozens of prototypes after a $5 million pre‑seed round. Benchmark’s investment marks the firm’s first bet on a pure defense startup, reflecting a shift in VC interest after Ukraine and Iran conflicts strained U.S. missile supplies. Furientis plans to build 1,000 systems a year by using readily available components, offering the Pentagon a cheaper alternative to traditional high‑cost interceptors.
key_points: Benchmark invests $25M seed in Furientis, its first pure defense startup bet.
Furientis, valued at $125M, has a Pentagon contract and has launched dozens of prototypes with only $5M pre‑seed.
The startup aims to produce 1,000 low‑cost interceptor missiles annually using readily available parts, addressing U.S. missile shortages.

posts.title: Vinod Khosla believes ex-DeepMind engineer's Wajo will win agent market on trust | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta
posts.summary: Vinod Khosla has publicly backed former DeepMind engineer Shivani Poddar’s startup Wajo, citing the company’s focus on trust as the key differentiator in a crowded personal‑agent market dominated by Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dot, and Instinct. Wajo’s Fo agent can schedule tasks, make calls, book services, and even create virtual credit cards while keeping user data hidden from third parties, and it has already grown 10× since its late‑September launch and operates in 107 countries. The startup has secured backing from Jeff Dean and Gokul Rajaram, and it is actively addressing privacy and safety through features like a trusted‑contact list and a patent‑pending virtual card system. Khosla’s endorsement signals that trust‑centric design may become a decisive factor for consumers choosing AI assistants.
key_points: Vinod Khosla backs Wajo for its trust‑first architecture
Wajo’s Fo agent handles calls, bookings, and virtual card payments while protecting user data
The startup has grown 10× since launch and operates in 107 countries
Backing from Jeff Dean and Gokul Rajaram underscores industry confidence

posts.title: Exclusive: Glimpse wants to give hardware companies an X-ray view of every critical part | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant
posts.summary: Glimpse has unveiled a software platform that can accelerate CT scanning of battery cells by 10 to 30 times, allowing manufacturers to inspect tens of thousands of cells per day instead of just a handful. The company’s new Explore product extends this high‑speed, deep‑learning‑powered image analysis to other sectors such as aerospace, automotive, electronics, and medical devices, helping them spot defects faster. Glimpse already serves over 100 customers—including Anker, Lucid, and the U.S. Navy—and reports mid‑seven‑figure revenue, while its Scan‑On‑Demand service lets firms ship parts to Boston or San Francisco for rapid inspection without buying expensive scanners.
key_points: Glimpse’s software boosts CT scan throughput 10–30×, enabling tens of thousands of battery cells to be inspected daily.
The Explore platform applies the same deep‑learning image processing to aerospace, automotive, electronics, and medical device quality control.
Customers can ship parts to Glimpse’s Scan‑On‑Demand centers, expanding access to high‑speed scanning without purchasing equipment.
The startup has more than 100 customers and generates mid‑seven‑figure revenue, indicating strong market traction.

posts.title: Mirror Particle is building a ‘world model’ of human behavior | TechCrunch
posts.author: Rebecca Bellan
posts.summary: Mirror Particle is developing a world model that simulates how humans change over time, arguing that large language models are too static to predict real behavior. The San Francisco startup uses longitudinal data and revealed actions, combining client data, social media, and current events to give brands not just predictions but the motivations behind them. In an early pilot, the company discovered that a pet‑food brand’s sales plateau was due to perception, not packaging imagery. Mirror Particle has raised an angel round, is close to closing its first venture round, and will compete in TechCrunch’s Startup Battlefield 2026.
key_points: Mirror Particle rejects LLMs in favor of a dynamic world model that tracks how people change over time
The engine relies on longitudinal data and revealed behavior to provide brands actionable insights and the underlying motivations
An early pilot with a pet‑food brand revealed that perception, not imagery, was the sales bottleneck
The startup is near closing its first venture round and will showcase its technology at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026

posts.title: Type One Energy raised $200M to build a fusion power plant by 2034 | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant
posts.summary: Type One Energy, a Knoxville‑based fusion startup, closed a $200 million Series B round to accelerate the construction of its first 400‑megawatt commercial fusion plant, which the company aims to bring online by 2034. The funding will help the firm move closer to a breakthrough while keeping capital requirements lower than many competitors by adopting an integrator model that outsources most component manufacturing to a curated network of suppliers. Key partners include AECOM for engineering, the Tennessee Valley Authority’s Bull Run site for initial devices, and Commonwealth Fusion Systems for high‑temperature superconducting magnet technology. The round was led by Breakthrough Energy Ventures and Clutterbuck Capital, with participation from Lowercarbon Capital, Siemens Energy Ventures, and SiteGround Capital, following an earlier $82.5 million Series A.
key_points: Type One Energy raised $200 million in Series B to fund a 400‑MW fusion plant slated for 2034
The company uses an integrator model, outsourcing most parts to reduce capital and manufacturing risk
Partnerships include AECOM, TVA’s Bull Run site, and Commonwealth Fusion Systems for magnet tech
Investors include Breakthrough Energy Ventures, Clutterbuck Capital, Lowercarbon Capital, Siemens Energy Ventures, and SiteGround Capital

posts.title: Bluesky wants to give you your own domain on the open web | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider announced the company has applied to ICANN to create a new top‑level domain called ".bsky", which would let users shorten handles such as @sarahp.bsky.social to sarahp.bsky. If approved, the new suffix could enable richer personal home pages and give users more control over their online identity. ICANN will publish the applications on Oct. 7 2026 and the process is expected to take 18‑24 months, but Bluesky has said it will not sell or monetize the domains. The move reflects Bluesky’s commitment to an open web and its belief that users should own rather than rent their digital presence.
key_points: Bluesky applied for a new ".bsky" top‑level domain
The domain could shorten handles and enable richer user profiles
ICANN will review the application on Oct. 7 2026 with an 18‑24 month timeline
Bluesky will not monetize the domains, supporting an open‑web philosophy

posts.title: Exclusive: Flai's AI dealership software is booking 50,000 appointments per month | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Flai’s AI‑powered dealership software is now booking 50,000 appointments per month across sales and service, driving a reported 20‑fold increase in revenue for its clients. The company, which has expanded to work with more than ten of the top 50 dealer groups in the U.S., just closed a $27 million Series A led by Base10 Partners and backed by Toyota’s venture arm, Y Combinator and First Round Capital. Flai’s rapid deployment—going live in a dealership 10 days after signing—and a 20‑minute response policy have spurred strong word‑of‑mouth referrals, helping the startup grow to about 40 employees. posts.title: OpenAI will start watermarking ChatGPT's text in the EU | TechCrunch

posts.title: Tesla sustains its EV sales momentum despite US troubles | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Tesla delivered more than 480,000 electric vehicles in the third quarter, surpassing Wall Street forecasts and its own optimistic estimates, even as U.S. sales fell about 20% year‑over‑year. The company offset the domestic decline with a rebound in Europe and China, expanding production capacity at its German plant to meet growing demand. Meanwhile, CEO Elon Musk has shifted focus to new ventures such as the Cybercab, the Tesla Semi, a re‑revealed Roadster, and the Optimus humanoid robot, all backed by a newly secured $30 billion line of credit.
key_points: Q3 sales exceeded 480,000 vehicles, beating consensus forecasts
U.S. sales dropped roughly 20% YoY, prompting a shift to international markets
Tesla is expanding its German factory to capture rising European demand
The company secured up to $30 billion in credit to fund future projects

posts.title: Federal judge calls Flock ‘indiscriminate mass surveillance’ | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: A federal judge in Tulsa ruled that a sheriff’s deputy violated a woman’s Fourth Amendment rights by searching the Flock Safety database for her license plate without a warrant, deeming the search unconstitutional and ordering that all evidence obtained thereafter be suppressed as the fruit of a poisonous tree. Judge Sara Hill criticized Flock as a tool for indiscriminate mass surveillance, noting that it passively catalogs every vehicle’s location and can be accessed by law enforcement at any time. The decision joins a growing chorus of critics, with states like Florida and Texas announcing they will stop using the technology and Senator Bernie Sanders introducing the Block Flock Act to bar federal agencies from using automated license plate readers. Flock’s CEO, Garrett Langley, has apologized to victims and the company has reportedly offered voluntary buyouts amid cancellations of its services.
key_points: Judge Sara Hill ruled that a warrant was required before searching the Flock database, and that evidence obtained after the search must be suppressed as the fruit of a poisonous tree.
The ruling labeled Flock a form of indiscriminate mass surveillance, arguing that passive, continuous location tracking for law‑enforcement use is constitutionally problematic.

State governments such as Florida and Texas have announced they will discontinue use of Flock, and Senator Bernie Sanders has introduced the Block Flock Act to prohibit federal use of automated license‑plate readers.
Flock CEO Garrett Langley apologized to victims and the company has offered voluntary employee buyouts as it faces growing cancellations.

posts.title: Spotify billionaire’s body scan startup has come to America | TechCrunch
posts.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
posts.summary: Neko Health, a body‑scan startup co‑founded by Spotify CEO Daniel Ek and Hjalmar Nilsonne, has just opened its first U.S. location in New York after raising nearly $1 billion and building a waitlist of over 300,000 people. The company offers a one‑hour, $500 scan that uses AI‑powered computer vision to measure 55 biomarkers in blood, skin and metabolism, positioning itself as a low‑cost, accessible preventative‑care solution. Investors like Farooq Abbasi see the technology as a way to address the U.S. healthcare system’s high costs and low preventive‑care uptake, while the firm plans rapid expansion across the country. Neko still faces significant scaling and regulatory challenges, but its founders remain optimistic about attracting further venture capital and transforming preventive medicine.
key_points: Neko Health, co‑founded by Spotify CEO Daniel Ek, offers a $500 AI‑driven body scan measuring 55 biomarkers
The startup has raised nearly $1 billion, has a waitlist of 300,000+ and just opened a New York clinic
It aims to make preventative care affordable and accessible in the U.S., targeting rapid expansion
Scaling and regulatory approval remain major hurdles for the company

posts.title: OpenAI launches visual ads that appear alongside image generation results | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: OpenAI is rolling out visual display ads that will appear alongside images generated by ChatGPT, beginning this month in the United States with a limited test group of advertisers. The ads will be clearly labeled and will not influence the model’s responses, while OpenAI expands its measurement tools and partner ecosystem to include click attribution and brand‑suitability solutions. The company aims to monetize its free and low‑cost subscription tiers and eventually reach its 1.2 billion weekly users worldwide. The move could alter the user experience and may encourage casual users to upgrade to paid plans to avoid ads.
key_points: Visual ads will appear next to image generation results in ChatGPT, starting in the U.S. this month.
The ads are labeled, do not affect ChatGPT answers, and are part of a test group of advertisers.
OpenAI is expanding measurement and brand‑suitability partnerships, including click attribution and geo‑based experiments.
The strategy is to monetize free and low‑cost plans and eventually target all 1.2 billion weekly users globally.

posts.title: Google froze its open source bug bounty program due to a 'significant rise' in AI submissions | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: Google has paused its Open Source Software Vulnerability Rewards Program as of October 1, citing a significant rise in automated, largely invalid AI-generated submissions that overwhelmed engineers and maintainers. The company will provide an update in the first quarter of 2027, effectively suspending the program until then. While the pause is in effect, researchers are encouraged to participate in Google’s other bug bounty programs. This decision underscores growing concerns about AI‑generated “slop” undermining the quality and reliability of bug bounty ecosystems.
key_points: Google paused its Open Source Software Vulnerability Rewards Program on Oct. 1 due to a surge in invalid AI‑generated submissions.
The pause will last until at least Q1 2027, with an update planned for that period.
Researchers are urged to use other Google bug bounty programs while the open‑source program remains suspended.
The move highlights increasing worries that AI‑generated “slop” can erode the effectiveness of bug bounty initiatives.

posts.title: TechCrunch Mobility: Reining in robotaxis | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kirsten Korosec
posts.summary: California’s Senate Bill 1246, signed by Governor Gavin Newsom, introduces new safety and accountability rules for autonomous vehicles, aiming to reduce incidents where robotaxis impede traffic, enter crime scenes, or block emergency responders. The law requires AV companies such as Waymo, Tesla, and Zoox to provide on‑ground support to first responders, limits remote drivers to U.S.‑licensed operators, and mandates notification of local jurisdictions during system failures. Violations—including blocking police or firefighters for over 30 minutes—can trigger penalties, while local incident technicians must be available to assist with accidents and obstructions. The legislation will take effect in July 2028, and while it may not eliminate all disruptions, it is intended to increase accountability and improve emergency response times for robotaxis.
key_points: California’s Senate Bill 1246 imposes new safety and accountability rules for robotaxis, including penalties for blocking emergency responders.
AV companies must provide local support and can face fines if they fail to assist first responders or block police or firefighters for more than 30 minutes.
Remote drivers must be U.S.‑licensed and based in the United States, and companies must notify local jurisdictions during system failures.
The law will take effect in July 2028, aiming to reduce chaos and raise accountability for autonomous vehicle incidents.

posts.title: Amazon responds to data center backlash, says it no longer uses NDAs | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman announced that AWS has stopped using nondisclosure agreements with government agencies as part of a broader effort to address public concerns about data center projects. The statement comes amid a backlash that has led to moratoriums on large data center permits in states like New York and a growing list of over 100 moratoriums nationwide. Garman also refuted common myths about data centers, noting that direct water use is only 0.5% of U.S. industrial consumption, electricity costs are largely driven by aging grids, and emissions are minimal because generators run only about 10 hours a year. He highlighted that AWS has contributed more than $1 billion to communities where it operates and that the company now prioritizes transparency by eliminating NDAs in its government dealings.
key_points: AWS stops using NDAs with government agencies
AWS counters myths: water use 0.5%, electricity impact tied to grid, minimal emissions
Over $1 billion community contributions
Moratoriums on data center permits across U.S. states

posts.title: Trump unveils his new Super Intelligence Force | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: President Donald Trump announced the creation of a new Super Intelligence Force, a task force aimed at ensuring the United States remains a global leader in what he calls "super intelligence," a term he uses to rebrand artificial intelligence. The force will be chaired by National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton, with Vice Chairs including FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson, Undersecretary of War for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and OPM Director Scott Kupor. Within 120 days the task force is expected to deliver a report outlining the risks and opportunities of AI, while balancing the need to avoid overregulation and maintain competitive innovation. The initiative reflects Trump’s broader strategy to keep the U.S. ahead of rivals such as China in the emerging AI landscape.
key_points: President Trump has formed a Super Intelligence Force chaired by Jay Clayton to coordinate federal AI strategy
The task force must produce a 120‑day report on AI risks and opportunities
The initiative rebrands AI as "super intelligence" to emphasize its strategic importance
Vice Chairs include FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson, Undersecretary of War for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and OPM Director Scott Kupor

posts.title: All the AI agents that can live in your text messages | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lauren Forristal
posts.summary: TechCrunch reports on a wave of AI agents that operate directly through text messaging, eliminating the need for separate apps. The article highlights Instinct, which recently raised $1 billion to reach a $10 billion valuation, and other players such as Caddy, Fambot, and Folk that integrate with iMessage, RCS, and popular messaging platforms to schedule appointments, manage calendars, and perform real‑world tasks. These agents can remember context, connect to existing services, and even run code on private cloud infrastructure, offering users a seamless, hands‑free experience. While the convenience is clear, the growing autonomy of these assistants raises privacy and security concerns, especially as some provide dedicated email addresses and call‑making capabilities.
key_points: Instinct raised $1 billion in September 2026, valuing it at $10 billion
Caddy has been in public beta since April 2026 and works within iMessage and RCS
Fambot offers family‑centric scheduling via SMS and connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp
Folk runs on a private cloud, can execute multi‑step tasks, and offers a $8.33/month Pro plan

posts.title: OpenAI safety employee resigns, claiming the company’s ‘culture is broken’ | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: David Robinson, a long‑tenured safety lead at OpenAI, resigned and published an essay in The Atlantic accusing the company’s culture of being broken. He argues that OpenAI’s iterative deployment model inevitably produces large‑scale failures and calls for a safety regime comparable to nuclear power plants or busy airports, with multiple layers of redundancy and careful planning. Robinson also stresses that current alignment metrics are coarse and that the industry must address deeper cultural and structural issues before AI systems become more capable. OpenAI’s spokesperson said the firm is tightening security, pausing training when needed, and expanding third‑party evaluation, but the resignation highlights ongoing concerns about AI safety culture in Silicon Valley.
key_points: David Robinson resigned citing a broken culture at OpenAI
He calls for a nuclear‑plant‑style safety regime with multiple layers of redundancy
Robinson warns that current alignment metrics are coarse and deeper cultural changes are needed
OpenAI says it is tightening security and expanding third‑party evaluation

posts.title: Jack Dorsey's Bitchat disappears from app stores in India after government order | TechCrunch
posts.author: Jagmeet Singh
posts.summary: Jack Dorsey’s decentralized messaging app Bitchat has been removed from Apple’s App Store and Google Play in India after the government issued a Section 69A order to block the app. The notice also barred access to Bitchat’s TestFlight beta and its website, while a prior July order had forced GitHub to delete the app’s open‑source repositories. The ban follows a wave of internet shutdowns during youth protests over voter‑roll changes, during which Bitchat’s popularity surged as users turned to offline messaging. The move raises concerns among digital‑rights advocates about the legality of blocking software that can operate without internet connectivity.
key_points: India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology ordered Apple and Google to remove Bitchat from their stores under Section 69A of the IT Act.
Bitchat, a Bluetooth‑mesh messaging app that works offline, was also blocked on its website and had its GitHub repositories taken down earlier in July.
The ban coincided with internet shutdowns during protests over voter‑roll changes, a period when Bitchat’s downloads spiked to 85% of its global traffic.
Digital‑rights groups argue the order is unconstitutional because Bitchat’s architecture prevents law‑enforcement interception and it can operate during shutdowns.

posts.title: Meta wants your next gadget to be Muse-infused | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kirsten Korosec
posts.summary: Meta has launched Muse Gadgets, an open‑source hardware initiative that lets developers build devices that connect to its personal AI agent, Muse. The company is providing low‑level firmware, a Linux SDK, and example projects such as a color e‑ink display or an HDMI‑port stick, while also offering a Discord channel for community support. Meta has already built and distributed 5,000 Muse Home Link units—USB‑C devices that let Muse interface with home networks and smart appliances—to subscribers, with plans to ship them soon. The move is part of Meta’s broader strategy to extend Muse beyond consumer use, targeting small businesses and enterprises through new tools and a dedicated Meta Enterprise Platform.
key_points: Meta releases Muse Gadgets, an open‑source hardware kit for building devices that connect to its AI agent
The kit includes firmware, a Linux SDK, and example projects like e‑ink displays and HDMI sticks
Meta has built 5,000 Muse Home Link devices, free to subscribers, and will ship them shortly
The initiative supports Meta’s expansion of Muse into small‑business and enterprise markets

posts.title: Sanders introduces bill to ban the federal government from using Flock | TechCrunch
posts.author: Connie Loizos
posts.summary: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the Ban Flock Act, a bill that would prohibit federal agencies from using automatic license‑plate readers (ALPRs) or accessing data from ALPRs operated by local police or private companies. The legislation allows only toll‑collection uses and future Congress‑approved applications that limit data retention to 48 hours, and it would penalize state and local governments that fail to comply by cutting federal grant funding. Flock Safety, the largest U.S. ALPR vendor with more than 120,000 cameras and a monthly 20 billion vehicle‑read volume, is a key target of the bill, and the company has already reduced its default data‑retention period to seven days amid public pressure. Co‑sponsors include Representative Alexandria Ocasio‑Cortez and Senator Jeff Merkley, underscoring bipartisan concern over privacy and surveillance.
key_points: The Ban Flock Act bars federal use of ALPRs and data from them, with limited toll‑collection exceptions and a 48‑hour retention cap.
Flock Safety, the largest ALPR vendor, operates 120,000+ cameras and processes 20 billion vehicle reads per month.
State and local governments that do not comply could lose federal grant funding from five departments, including Justice and Homeland Security.
The bill is co‑sponsored by AOC and Jeff Merkley, reflecting bipartisan support for privacy reforms.

It excludes industry stages and roundtable sessions, but attendees can still use the app’s AI matchmaking to set up meetings. The offer ends once all 100 passes are claimed or the doors open, encouraging displaced workers to reconnect with the startup ecosystem.

Pass grants entry to the Expo Hall and networking tools but not stage sessions
The conference hosts over 10,000 attendees, including founders, investors, and tech leaders
Passes are limited; after 100 are sold or doors open, the offer ends

posts.title: One year later, Tesla and Musk still don't have a good definition of 'abundance' | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Elon Musk’s fourth Tesla Master Plan, unveiled on September 1, 2025, promises a future of "amazing abundance" that includes robotaxis, humanoid robots, and AI‑driven medical care, yet offers no concrete roadmap or metrics. The vision was used to justify a $1 trillion pay package for Musk in 2025, with Tesla’s regulatory filings tying the payout to ambitious product targets such as 20 million vehicles and 10 million Full Self‑Driving subscriptions. Shareholders were encouraged to support the slogan in a letter that framed it as a pathway to global prosperity, while Tesla applied to trademark "amazing abundance" for a wide range of merchandise. Despite the grand rhetoric, practical details remain scarce and the term continues to function largely as a marketing catch‑phrase rather than a measurable strategy.
key_points: Musk’s Master Plan IV promises "amazing abundance" without concrete details
Tesla’s $1 trillion pay package is tied to vague vision and product targets
Shareholders were urged to endorse the slogan as a path to prosperity
Tesla trademarked "amazing abundance" for various products

posts.title: Sean Parker is rebuilding Stability AI around music | TechCrunch
posts.author: Connie Loizos
posts.summary: Sean Parker, the Napster co‑founder, has re‑entered the music industry by steering Stability AI—an image‑generation startup that survived an $80 million rescue—toward becoming a premier AI toolmaker for music professionals. In late August, Stability secured $76 million in new funding from Sony, Warner, Universal and others, who also licensed their catalogs to train the models. The company has released three audio models and AI music‑editing software that can generate full instrumental tracks or snippets from text prompts, with an upcoming update planned to let users hum or beatbox to guide the output. Parker’s approach signals a shift from his earlier “forgiveness” strategy to a more collaborative, rule‑compliant model in the creative tech space.
key_points: Parker and CEO Prem Akkaraju are transforming Stability AI into an AI music‑tool platform after a $80 million rescue and a $76 million new funding round from major record labels.
The new audio models can generate full tracks or snippets from text prompts, and an upcoming update will allow users to steer music by humming or beatboxing.

posts.title: Medical records giant Epic pauses product development to fix security bugs that risk patients' data | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: Epic, the software giant behind the MyChart patient portal, has halted most product development for about six weeks to address security bugs uncovered by Anthropic’s AI model Mythos. The flaws could let unauthorized users view patient records without leaving logs, raising concerns about data privacy and potential undetected tampering. Epic’s MyChart platform manages over 320 million patient records nationwide, and the company does not store the data itself, but a vulnerability could expose it across multiple U.S. healthcare systems. The pause reflects growing fears that AI‑driven vulnerability discovery may accelerate cyberattacks on sensitive medical data.
key_points: Epic has paused product development for roughly six weeks to fix security bugs revealed by an AI model.
The bugs could allow outsiders to access patient records in MyChart without logging the intrusion.
Epic’s MyChart platform holds more than 320 million patient records across U.S. hospitals and clinics.
The move underscores the heightened risk of AI‑accelerated vulnerability discovery in healthcare software.

posts.title: Rivian's R2 just helped it set a new sales record | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Rivian reported its highest ever third‑quarter vehicle deliveries, shipping 19,248 units—about 45% more than the same period last year—thanks largely to the launch of its new, more affordable R2 SUV. The R2, priced just under $60,000, is expected to sell 20,000 to 25,000 units by year‑end, potentially making it the fastest‑selling U.S. EV after Tesla’s Model Y. Rivian plans to hit 65,000 to 70,000 total sales this year, a record, and is expanding production with a new Atlanta plant that could reach 300,000 vehicles annually. The company also partnered with Uber for robotaxi versions of the R2, pushing its profitability target to 2027 to invest more in autonomy.
key_points: Q3 deliveries hit 19,248, a 45% year‑over‑year increase driven by the R2 SUV launch
R2 is priced under $60k with a target of 20,000‑25,000 units by year‑end, aiming to become one of the fastest‑selling U.S. EVs
Rivian expects 65,000‑70,000 total sales this year, its best record, supported by a new Atlanta factory with 300,000‑vehicle capacity

posts.title: Blackstone’s Jas Khaira joins Disrupt 2026 | TechCrunch
posts.author: TechCrunch Events

He will discuss Blackstone’s recent $600 million equity investment in Indian AI infrastructure firm Neysa and the $1.5 billion joint venture backing Anthropic’s Ode, illustrating the scale of capital required for AI infrastructure and talent. Khaira will outline the investor criteria that separate fast‑growing startups from those that can endure, emphasizing the importance of strategic capital use over simply raising more money. The session is part of a larger event that will host over 10,000 founders, investors and tech leaders, offering networking, deal‑making and insights into building AI companies for the long haul.

Khaira will explain the investor criteria that distinguish sustainable AI companies from those that only grow quickly
Disrupt 2026 provides a platform for founders to network with investors, customers and partners in a large, multi‑stage event
Capital for AI goes beyond product development to include compute, data centers and talent acquisition

posts.title: Clay’s Kareem Amin joins Disrupt 2026 | TechCrunch
posts.author: TechCrunch Events
posts.summary: Clay co‑founder Kareem Amin will headline TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 with a talk titled "The GTM Engineer: How AI Created Tech’s Next Big Job Category," outlining how AI and automation are reshaping go‑to‑market workflows and creating a new engineering discipline. Kareem Amin’s Disrupt talk will help founders decide between hiring more staff or building AI‑driven systems

posts.title: Rivian issues R2 recall for poorly tightened battery packs | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Rivian has issued a recall for about 14 of its R2 SUVs after discovering that fasteners on the high‑voltage battery pack were under‑torqued, which could cause a loss of power while driving. The company will inspect and repair or replace the affected components at no cost to owners, and it reports no accidents or injuries linked to the defect. This is the second R2 recall, following a backup‑camera software issue last month, and comes as Rivian pushes to ship 20,000–25,000 units by year‑end to reach profitability. The recall underscores the company’s focus on safety and its aggressive production ramp for the mass‑market electric SUV.
key_points: Rivian recalls roughly 14 R2 SUVs due to under‑torqued battery fasteners
No customer reports of accidents or injuries have been filed
This is the second recall for the R2, the first involving a backup‑camera software update
The R2 launch is critical to Rivian’s profitability and mass‑market strategy

posts.title: Apple says it's tightening macOS 'Full Disk Access' controls due to new risks from AI agents | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Apple has announced new controls for macOS's Full Disk Access setting after reports that AI agents like Meta’s Muse could read private messages without explicit permission. The changes aim to require explicit user action before granting an app the ability to read files, mail, messages, and browsing history, addressing growing risks as desktop AI becomes more autonomous. The move follows Wired’s report of a ChatGPT Mac app flaw that could expose sensitive data and a journalist’s claim that Muse accessed private messages. Apple’s update emphasizes informed consent rather than limiting permissions, though the company did not comment on the changes.
key_points: Apple introduces stricter controls on macOS Full Disk Access to curb AI agents reading private data
The new policy requires explicit user action before an app can access files, mail, messages, and browsing history
The change follows incidents involving Meta’s Muse and a ChatGPT Mac app flaw that raised privacy concerns

posts.title: Circuit Breaker Labs hopes to make AI safer for your kids (and you) | TechCrunch
posts.author: Julie Bort
posts.summary: Circuit Breaker Labs, a 2026 Startup Battlefield finalist, is developing a testing platform that uses hyper‑realistic user simulations to evaluate AI models for psychologically harmful interactions across diverse ages, languages, and slang. The sibling founders, motivated by a 2024 lawsuit in which a teen’s suicide was linked to a Character.AI chatbot, built an "army of crash‑test dummies" that run tens of thousands of simulated conversations daily and score models with a proprietary, auditable method. The startup is already serving high‑risk mental‑health applications and plans to extend its framework to any AI that could foster parasocial relationships or other dangerous dynamics. By exposing safety vulnerabilities before deployment, Circuit Breaker Labs aims to build trust and make AI safer for children and adults alike.
key_points: Circuit Breaker Labs uses hyper‑realistic simulations to test AI for psychological safety across diverse demographics
The founders were driven by a 2024 lawsuit where a teen’s suicide was linked to a Character.AI chatbot
The platform runs tens of thousands of daily simulated interactions and provides auditable safety scores
It currently serves high‑risk mental‑health applications and aims to broaden to other AI contexts

posts.title: Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery to become Skydance | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lauren Forristal
posts.summary: Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery will merge into a new entity called Skydance once the $110 billion deal closes on October 6. The combined company will own Paramount+, HBO Max, CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central, Food Network, and major franchises such as The Lord of the Rings, Game of Thrones, the DC Universe, and Yellowstone. CEO David Ellison said the Paramount and Warner Bros. brands will remain central while the new name gives the company its own identity. The merger follows a legal battle and a settlement with state attorneys general that cleared the way for the deal.
